paragraphs: A streaming algorithm processes incoming data while retaining a limited summary. This becomes harder when an adversary chooses future inputs after observing earlier outputs. Those outputs can reveal information about the algorithm’s randomness, allowing the adversary to exploit dependencies that would not arise in a fixed, independently chosen stream.

The paper shows that many algorithms based on importance sampling remain reliable under this adaptive interaction. It develops robust methods for regression, clustering, and related numerical tasks, including low-rank approximation and subspace embedding. For regression and the other numerical linear algebra problems, the analysis uses a setting in which matrix rows arrive sequentially.

The authors also establish robustness of the merge-and-reduce strategy, extending the result to streaming coreset constructions for several clustering and matrix problems. These guarantees can apply without new algorithmic implementations. Experiments support robustness against the attacks studied and show failures of some common alternatives. The contribution is therefore both a theoretical explanation of existing methods’ resilience and a route to robust streaming algorithms.
neurips-2021-adversarial-robustness-of-s.tldr: Importance sampling and merge-and-reduce provide adversarial robustness for a broad range of streaming learning algorithms.

paragraphs: Combining causal evidence from multiple sources requires more than producing a single treatment-effect estimate. Sources can differ in sample size and quality, and their data may arise from different causal graphs. The paper studies how to combine this evidence while accounting for uncertainty in the estimated average effect on a target variable.

Its framework, Bayesian Causal Mean Processes, combines probabilistic integration with kernel mean embeddings. These tools represent distributions associated with interventions in a mathematical feature space while incorporating uncertainty within each causal graph. The central idea is to make uncertainty part of the data-fusion calculation, rather than treating every source’s contribution as equally well established.

The authors evaluate the usefulness of these uncertainty estimates through causal Bayesian optimisation, where estimates inform the search for interventions. They report improvements over state-of-the-art methods in that task. This connects uncertainty quantification to a practical decision process: the framework is intended to support better intervention choices as well as estimates of causal effects.
neurips-2021-bayesimp-uncertainty-quanti.tldr: BayesIMP combines causal evidence across sources while tracking uncertainty, improving the reported causal Bayesian optimisation results.

paragraphs: High-dimensional learning can be difficult because the amount of information needed often grows sharply with the number of inputs. This paper investigates a different source of effective simplicity: the target function may vary unevenly across directions. Some inputs can require detailed modelling while others have much smoother effects, even without low-dimensional structure in the data.

The analysis uses anisotropic Besov spaces, function classes that describe direction-dependent smoothness. The authors show that deep learning’s approximation and estimation errors depend on an average of the smoothness parameters across directions. Consequently, sufficiently strong anisotropy can allow the method to avoid the curse of dimensionality under the conditions studied.

The paper also examines minimax optimality and compares deep learning with kernel methods and, more broadly, linear estimators. Its results show better dependence on input dimensionality when the target has anisotropic smoothness, together with adaptive rates when smoothness varies across locations. The explanation for favourable learning behaviour therefore comes from the structure of the target function itself.
neurips-2021-deep-learning-is-adaptive-t.tldr: Deep learning can adapt to uneven target-function smoothness, reducing dimensionality costs without assuming low-dimensional input data.

paragraphs: Few-shot recognition becomes harder when the dataset used for initial training differs substantially from the target domain. Unlabelled target images offer useful information, but a fixed teacher trained on the base domain may interpret them through an unsuitable set of learned categories. This paper replaces that fixed teacher with one that changes during training.

The method trains a student to match a teacher’s predictions across differently augmented versions of the same unlabelled image. The teacher sees a weakly augmented version, while the student sees a strongly augmented version. Teacher parameters follow an exponential moving average of student parameters, creating an evolving source of consistency targets.

The resulting representations adapt to target classes that were absent from pretraining. On BSCD-FSL, the authors report improvements over the current state of the art of 4.4% for one-shot and 3.6% for five-shot classification. They also report competitive performance within a single domain. These findings support dynamic distillation as a useful way to exploit unlabelled data across a domain shift.
neurips-2021-dynamic-distillation-networ.tldr: An evolving teacher and augmentation consistency improve few-shot recognition across domains using unlabelled images.

paragraphs: A Bayesian neural network places a probability distribution over its weights, which induces a distribution over its outputs before observing training data. Infinite-width networks have a well-understood Gaussian description under Gaussian weight priors. Finite networks can have non-Gaussian output distributions, and this paper derives exact expressions for a class of those distributions.

The results concern individual input examples in finite, fully connected feedforward networks. For deep linear networks, the output prior can be written using the Meijer G-function. For ReLU networks, it becomes a mixture of linear-network priors with smaller widths, reflecting the different possible numbers of active units in each layer.

This mixture description connects the activation pattern of a finite network to its output uncertainty. The exact formulas also unify earlier descriptions based on tail decay and large-width behaviour. Their scope is marginal priors at individual inputs: the contribution is an exact account of this aspect of finite networks, rather than a new empirical claim that finite networks always outperform infinite ones.
neurips-2021-exact-marginal-prior-distri.tldr: The paper derives exact single-input output priors for a class of finite linear and ReLU Bayesian networks.

paragraphs: Random forests can assign importance scores to input variables across an entire dataset. Such global scores describe overall predictive relevance, but they do not directly explain how relevance varies between individual examples. This paper connects the familiar Mean Decrease of Impurity measure, or MDI, with methods that attribute importance at the individual-instance level.

The authors first show that global MDI scores correspond to Shapley values under certain conditions. That qualification matters: the result does not identify every random forest’s importance scores with Shapley values automatically. They then derive a local MDI measure that has a natural relationship to the global measure and to a new definition of local feature relevance.

The analysis further connects these local scores with Shapley values and discusses their relationship to existing measures. Experiments on classification and regression problems illustrate the proposed quantities. Together, the results provide a theoretical bridge between dataset-level importance and instance-level relevance, helping place two approaches to explaining tree models within a connected framework.
neurips-2021-from-global-to-local-mdi-va.tldr: The paper develops local MDI feature importance and establishes conditional connections between MDI and Shapley values.

paragraphs: Retrieving images of a particular object requires distinguishing genuine matches from images that merely look similar. Spatial verification helps by checking spatial information, but existing query expansion and diffusion methods struggle to propagate that information efficiently through ordinary graphs with scalar edge weights. This can reduce either the completeness or the accuracy of retrieval results.

The paper introduces a hypergraph framework that propagates spatial information during a query. It also uses community selection based on the structure of an image graph to assess the initial search results. This step supplies suitable starting points for propagation without requiring heavy spatial verification computations to establish those starting points.

The two components address complementary parts of retrieval: selecting reliable initial matches and spreading spatial evidence through the database. Experiments on ROxford and RParis show significant improvements over existing query expansion and diffusion methods. The reported findings support using richer relationships and graph structure to improve object retrieval in these evaluated settings.
neurips-2021-hypergraph-propagation-and-.tldr: Hypergraph propagation and graph-based community selection improve object retrieval by spreading spatial evidence from better starting points.

paragraphs: Autoregressive image models generate content sequentially, so a patch typically depends on patches already produced above or to its left. This ordering delays access to much of the scene and handles the image at a single scale. ImageBART introduces a hierarchy that makes broader scene context available while progressively generating finer detail.

The method combines autoregressive modelling with multinomial diffusion. A forward process repeatedly removes information to produce increasingly coarse images, and a learned Markov chain reverses that process. At each reconstruction stage, the autoregressive model draws on the preceding, coarser stage, allowing context to extend beyond the local generation order.

Experiments report gains over the compared autoregressive, continuous diffusion, and latent-variable models. The approach also supports control over synthesis and a tradeoff between compression rate and reconstruction accuracy while retaining visually plausible outputs. Its main contribution is a way to combine sequential generation with a coarse-to-fine view of the scene, so detailed synthesis can use context established earlier at broader scales.
neurips-2021-imagebart-bidirectional-con.tldr: ImageBART combines autoregressive generation with multinomial diffusion to build images using progressively finer, scene-wide context.

paragraphs: Learning features whose predictive relationships remain stable across environments is a major strategy for handling distribution shifts. Yet invariance-based methods can fail in classification even when invariant features contain all the information needed to determine the label. This paper asks whether those failures arise from imperfect methods or from limits of invariance itself.

The authors revisit assumptions that support generalisation guarantees in linear regression and compare them with linear classification. They show that classification requires substantially stronger restrictions on distribution shifts; without suitable restrictions, out-of-distribution generalisation is impossible. They also establish that invariance alone remains insufficient even when appropriate shift restrictions are imposed.

The proposed remedy combines invariance with a form of information bottleneck constraint, which limits information retained in the representation. The theory shows that this combination addresses key failures when invariant features fully determine labels while preserving existing successes when they do not. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of an approach built from both principles, supporting a more qualified account of when invariance can help.
neurips-2021-invariance-principle-meets-.tldr: Combining invariance with an information bottleneck addresses classification failures that invariance alone cannot resolve under suitable shift restrictions.

paragraphs: Compact neural representations are useful both for learning features and for removing unnecessary network structure. The paper identifies training instability and an additional fine-tuning stage as problems in existing structured pruning methods. It proposes DiscriminAtive Masking, or DAM, to learn which neurons to retain while refining their weights in the same training process.

DAM preferentially trains some neurons while gradually masking others out. This makes selection and weight refinement parts of a single stage, avoiding the need for post-convergence fine-tuning in the proposed method. The authors also show a direct theoretical relationship between its objective and minimising the L0 norm of the masking layer, which measures the number of nonzero entries.

The approach is evaluated across dimensionality reduction, recommendation, graph representation learning, and structured pruning for image classification. The authors report strong performance across these applications. The contribution therefore links a practical training procedure with an explicit sparsity objective, using the same mechanism to encourage compact representations and to remove neurons during training.
neurips-2021-learning-compact-representa.tldr: DAM jointly selects neurons and refines weights through gradual masking, producing compact networks without a separate fine-tuning stage.

paragraphs: A matching platform must pair participants while learning what those participants prefer. During this learning process, uncertain preferences prevent the platform from guaranteeing classical stability. The paper develops a framework for measuring and reducing the distance from equilibrium while preferences are still being learned, rather than assuming they are already known.

Its main setting allows transferable utilities: the platform chooses both matches and monetary transfers between participants. The authors introduce an incentive-aware objective that measures how far an outcome is from equilibrium. They then formulate preference learning as a stochastic multi-armed bandit problem and study how its difficulty depends on the structure of those preferences.

The algorithm applies optimism under uncertainty to a primal-dual formulation of matching with transfers. This means using plausible favourable estimates while coordinating the matching and transfer decisions. The resulting regret bounds are near optimal for the analysed objective. These results provide a principled way to assess progress towards stable market outcomes during learning, without claiming exact classical stability at every intermediate decision.
neurips-2021-learning-equilibria-in-matc.tldr: An incentive-aware bandit framework learns matches and monetary transfers with near-optimal regret measured by distance from equilibrium.

paragraphs: Online change detection aims to recognise a shift soon after it happens while avoiding false alarms. This paper studies that problem when local differential privacy prevents the statistician from seeing raw observations. The challenge is to detect changes from privacy-protected information without losing control over either detection speed or mistaken alerts.

The main setting is multivariate nonparametric regression. Each observation contains a feature vector and a response, and the quantity that may change is the expected response given those features. The authors develop algorithms that satisfy the privacy constraint, control false alarm probability, and achieve minimax rate-optimal detection delay in the studied problem.

They also derive the optimal rate without privacy constraints, providing a benchmark for quantifying the cost of privacy. Those non-private results are themselves new contributions. A simpler problem involving changes in a univariate mean serves as a blueprint for the more complex analysis. Together, the results characterise how quickly changes can be detected while respecting local privacy.
neurips-2021-locally-private-online-chan.tldr: The paper gives locally private change detectors with controlled false alarms and minimax rate-optimal detection delays.

paragraphs: Adapting a trained model to an unlabelled target domain often assumes access to the original source data. That access can be difficult because of privacy, portability, or transmission concerns. This paper instead studies adaptation using a source-trained model without the source dataset, drawing on historical models to retain useful information during adaptation.

Historical contrastive learning has two components. The first contrasts target-image embeddings produced by the current model and historical models. It encourages representations that distinguish individual target examples while preserving the source hypothesis. The second assigns pseudo-labels to target samples and adjusts their weights according to prediction consistency across current and historical models.

These components support complementary goals: keeping individual examples distinguishable and learning representations that separate categories. Historical predictions provide a reference throughout both processes, compensating for the absence of source observations. The authors report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods across several visual tasks and setups. The results support model history as a useful resource for adapting to an unlabelled domain.
neurips-2021-model-adaptation-historical.tldr: Historical contrastive learning uses current and past models to adapt to unlabelled target data without accessing source data.

paragraphs: Population-based game solvers repeatedly decide which opponents to train against and how to respond to them. These decisions often follow manually designed game-theoretic rules. Neural Auto-Curricula, or NAC, instead learns the update procedure through interaction with two-player zero-sum games, making the training curriculum itself an object of optimisation.

NAC represents opponent selection with neural networks and best-response learning with optimisation subroutines. Meta-gradient descent adjusts their parameters, with both players seeking to reduce exploitability. The learned procedure therefore shapes the mixture of opponents and the response process according to how those choices affect the players’ vulnerability to exploitation.

Across the games studied, the discovered algorithms are competitive with or outperform state-of-the-art population-based solvers. The authors also demonstrate transfer from smaller to larger games: a procedure trained on Kuhn Poker outperforms PSRO on Leduc Poker. These findings support the possibility of learning useful game-solving rules from interactions, while the demonstrated generalisation concerns the specific transfers evaluated in the paper.
neurips-2021-neural-auto-curricula-in-tw.tldr: NAC learns opponent-selection and response-update rules through game interaction, achieving competitive results and demonstrated transfer between poker games.

paragraphs: Training with augmented images can improve robustness to noise, warping, and colour changes. However, strong results on a corruption benchmark do not by themselves explain which new corruptions a model will handle. This paper investigates how the similarity between training augmentations and test-time corruptions relates to the robustness gains observed.

The authors construct a feature space for image transformations and introduce Minimal Sample Distance to measure relationships between augmentations and corruptions within it. They find a strong correlation between transformation similarity and performance. This provides a way to examine whether an augmentation’s apparent robustness benefit is associated with resemblance to the transformations used for evaluation.

They then evaluate recent augmentations on corruptions selected to be perceptually dissimilar from ImageNet-C in that feature space and observe substantial robustness degradation. The results suggest that perceptually similar training augmentations can improve test error, while benefits may transfer poorly beyond the existing benchmark. The contribution is both a measurement tool and evidence that corruption similarity matters when interpreting robustness improvements.
neurips-2021-on-interaction-between-augm.tldr: Robustness gains correlate with augmentation–corruption similarity and can weaken substantially on perceptually different corruptions.

paragraphs: Many reinforcement-learning systems assume a reward signal at every step, but judging individual actions can be harder than judging a complete outcome. This paper studies the extreme case in which the learner receives just one binary assessment at the end of an episode: whether its full trajectory was good or bad.

The theoretical setting assumes those trajectory labels are generated by an unknown parametric model. That assumption supplies structure for learning from the sparse feedback. The authors develop an algorithm that is efficient both statistically and computationally, showing that the learner can make progress despite receiving no separate reward assessment for each intermediate action.

The algorithm achieves sublinear regret, meaning its cumulative performance shortfall grows more slowly than the number of learning episodes. Thus, average regret decreases as learning continues in the analysed setting. The result establishes a route to efficient learning from whole-trajectory judgements, motivated by applications such as robotics and self-driving where such judgements may be easier to obtain than detailed rewards.
neurips-2021-on-the-theory-of-reinforcem.tldr: Efficient reinforcement learning with sublinear regret is possible from one binary label per episode under the studied parametric feedback model.

paragraphs: Many learning problems describe an object through a set of features, such as those arising from point clouds, graphs, or images. A model needs to aggregate that set into a fixed-dimensional representation. This paper proposes a pooling mechanism that gives the aggregation a geometric interpretation by treating set elements as samples from a probability distribution.

The method builds an end-to-end trainable Euclidean embedding for sliced-Wasserstein distance. Its central move is to represent a collection through the distribution suggested by its elements, using that distributional viewpoint to construct the pooled vector. Because the embedding is trainable, pooling can be learned together with the surrounding model for the task being solved.

The authors evaluate the method on point-cloud, graph, and image classification, reporting better performance than existing set-representation approaches in those evaluations. The range of tasks supports its intended use as a generic pooling component. Its contribution joins a fixed-size output suitable for learning systems with an explicit geometric basis for representing the input set.
neurips-2021-pooling-by-sliced-wasserste.tldr: A trainable sliced-Wasserstein embedding pools feature sets into fixed-size vectors and improves the reported classification results.

paragraphs: Federated learning brings together clients whose data and computing resources can differ substantially. A single shared model may not accommodate both kinds of variation. QuPeD addresses them jointly by allowing each client to learn a personalised compressed model, with its own dimensions, structure, and quantisation parameters, while still participating in collaborative training.

The method first formulates quantised model learning through a relaxed optimisation problem that also learns the quantisation values. It then introduces knowledge-distillation losses into client objectives so differently sized and differently precise models can collaborate through a global model. This connects local compression requirements with the information shared during federated learning.

The authors develop alternating proximal gradient updates for the resulting objective and analyse their convergence properties. Numerical evaluations show QuPeD outperforming the compared personalised federated methods, FedAvg, and independent local training across various heterogeneous settings. These findings support combining personalisation and compression within one training framework, rather than requiring all participating clients to use the same model configuration.
neurips-2021-quped-quantized-personaliza.tldr: QuPeD combines learned quantisation, personalised models, and knowledge distillation for federated clients with differing data and resources.

paragraphs: An ensemble benefits from having models that behave differently, but independently trained networks can converge to similar functions. Adding more members may then offer little improvement and can leave uncertainty estimates inadequate, especially for unfamiliar data. This paper investigates whether explicitly discouraging such functional collapse can improve the foundations of ensemble training.

The authors add a kernel-based repulsive term to the update rule, encouraging members to remain diverse. They study repulsion in both weight space and function space. The theoretical result connects the resulting training dynamics to a Wasserstein gradient flow of the Kullback–Leibler divergence relative to the true posterior.

This connection gives the modified dynamics a Bayesian interpretation beyond independent maximum a posteriori estimation. Diversity is therefore tied to an inference objective, rather than serving only as a practical preference among ensemble members. The paper also compares repulsive ensembles with standard ensembles and Bayesian baselines on synthetic and real-world prediction tasks, examining the behaviour of the proposed modification empirically.
neurips-2021-repulsive-deep-ensembles-ar.tldr: Kernel-based repulsion maintains ensemble diversity and connects ensemble training dynamics to Bayesian posterior inference.

paragraphs: Some theoretical guarantees attributed to residual networks concern architectures that differ from standard vision ResNets. This paper makes one difference explicit by defining ResNEsts, which remove nonlinearities from the final residual representation before the affine output layer. That change exposes a linear estimation structure and clarifies which models the guarantees actually describe.

The authors identify a coupling between learned basis functions and prediction weights that limits ResNEsts. An augmented architecture separates those roles and guarantees that adding a block does not worsen performance. It also supplies empirical-risk lower bounds for a ResNEst using corresponding bases. Sufficiently wide ResNEsts with bottleneck blocks recover the desired non-degradation property for a fixed set of basis elements.

The paper also proposes DenseNEsts, inspired by densely connected networks. Every DenseNEst can be represented as a wide bottleneck ResNEst, while DenseNEsts obtain the desirable property without special architectural redesign. These are representation and training-performance guarantees under the stated constructions; they explain how architecture affects feature reuse and the benefits available from additional blocks.
neurips-2021-resnests-and-densenests-blo.tldr: ResNEsts and DenseNEsts clarify architectural conditions under which adding blocks preserves or improves training performance.

paragraphs: Class-incremental learning introduces new categories over time while retaining only a limited number of past examples for replay. How that memory is divided can affect what the classifier remembers. This paper replaces static allocation rules with reinforced memory management, or RMM, a learned policy that adjusts memory allocation across phases and classes.

The policy makes decisions at two levels: it first splits memory between old and new classes, then allocates space to individual classes. Training such a policy directly is difficult because past and future datasets are unavailable during incremental learning. RMM handles this by learning on pseudo incremental tasks, such as tasks constructed from the initial phase’s data, before applying the policy to target tasks.

The authors integrate RMM into two existing replay-based methods and evaluate three benchmarks. In the reported 25-phase setting, POD+AANets improves by 3.6%, 4.4%, and 1.9% on CIFAR-100, ImageNet-Subset, and ImageNet-Full, respectively. These results support learned memory allocation as a useful component that can complement an existing incremental-learning method.
neurips-2021-rmm-reinforced-memory-manag.tldr: RMM learns how to divide replay memory across old, new, and individual classes, improving evaluated incremental-learning systems.

paragraphs: Video models need to capture both spatial detail and changes over time, but learning from high-resolution, long-duration inputs can require substantial memory. This paper decomposes a three-dimensional convolutional filter into spatial atoms, temporal atoms, and joint coefficients. The resulting three convolutional layers separate spatial and temporal learning while retaining their relationship.

The decomposition allows one set of atoms to be replaced with equally many atoms of different sizes while leaving the remaining components unchanged. The authors use temporal dilation to achieve tempo invariance. They also alternate training stages: one preserves full temporal resolution while reducing spatial resolution, and the other preserves full spatial resolution while reducing temporal resolution.

During each stage, the corresponding atoms and joint coefficients are learned while the other atoms stay fixed. Across multiple action-recognition datasets, this procedure substantially reduces model memory use and maintains comparable performance. It enables the evaluated deep 3D networks to learn high-spatial and long-temporal dependencies within limited computational resources, connecting the filter decomposition to a practical training strategy.
neurips-2021-spatiotemporal-joint-filter.tldr: Joint filter decomposition separates spatial and temporal video learning, reducing memory use while preserving comparable recognition performance.

paragraphs: Wider networks gain representational capacity, which can obscure whether width also has harmful effects once capacity is sufficient. This paper separates those issues using deep Gaussian processes, hierarchical nonparametric models that include neural networks within a broader framework. The aim is to isolate how width affects adaptability rather than merely how many functions can be represented.

The authors prove that increasing width makes even nonparametric deep Gaussian processes converge to Gaussian processes, effectively reducing their hierarchy without increasing representational power. Their posterior becomes less dependent on the data. Tail analysis also shows opposing effects: depth strengthens non-Gaussian behaviour, while width increasingly produces Gaussian behaviour.

The studied nonparametric models reach their best test performance at widths of one or two. Experiments with conventional L2-regularised networks show a related pattern: depending on the dataset, 500–1000 hidden units may be needed for sufficient capacity, after which additional width degrades performance. These findings support a qualified claim that excessive width can reduce adaptability in the models and settings examined.
neurips-2021-the-limitations-of-large-wi.tldr: Deep Gaussian process analysis shows how increasing width can reduce data adaptability and hurt performance after capacity is sufficient.

paragraphs: Universal approximation results suggest that a single hidden layer can approximate a broad range of functions. This paper examines a different question: which functions can a ReLU network represent exactly? That distinction matters because getting arbitrarily close to a function does not settle whether a particular architecture can express it without approximation.

The authors investigate whether adding layers strictly enlarges the class of exactly representable functions when network size is otherwise unrestricted. Removing size restrictions focuses attention on depth itself: the question is whether extra layers provide an expressive capability that cannot simply be replaced by more units at the existing depth.

The analysis draws on mixed-integer optimisation, polyhedral theory, and tropical geometry. It also provides upper bounds on the network sizes needed to represent functions in the hypothesis classes studied. The contribution develops a mathematical account of architecture-dependent expressiveness with potential algorithmic and statistical implications. The abstract frames the strict depth hierarchy as an investigated question, rather than claiming a complete resolution for every depth.
neurips-2021-towards-lower-bounds-on-the.tldr: The paper investigates how depth affects exact ReLU representation and derives size upper bounds for the studied function classes.

paragraphs: Probabilistic circuits combine structured probabilistic modelling with computation graphs that support efficient, exact inference. They can also use scalable neural-network-style parameter updates, but this flexibility can lead to overfitting. The paper develops regularisers specifically around the computations these models can perform efficiently, rather than relying only on techniques borrowed from other model families.

The first method, data softening, introduces uncertainty into the dataset in closed form and thereby implicitly regularises model parameters. The circuit’s tractability allows learning from the softened data in linear time. The second method regularises the exact entropy of the represented distribution directly, using a quantity that is generally difficult to compute for other density estimators.

Both techniques retain efficient computation-graph implementations. Across the evaluated probabilistic circuits, the authors report consistent generalisation improvements. Combined with a simple circuit structure, the methods achieve state-of-the-art results on 10 of 20 standard discrete density-estimation benchmarks. The findings show how tractable inference can support regularisation as well as prediction and probabilistic querying.
neurips-2021-tractable-regularization-of.tldr: Data softening and exact entropy regularisation exploit probabilistic circuits’ tractability to improve generalisation.
